<reason>Both sides were disciplined, closed-book honest, and format-compliant, and the clash narrowed cleanly. PRO set the dominant frame (what the marginal public dollar buys) and landed a vivid downside asymmetry: a failed apprenticeship year still pays wages, a failed college year leaves debt. CON, however, did more damage to the load-bearing parts of that case. First, it broke PRO's marginal-student story by pointing out that aid does not only recruit fence-sitters but rescues already-enrolled students from financial dropout, so the payoff is entrants times completion plus persisters converted — a mechanism PRO never rebutted, answering only with a demand for a number PRO also could not supply. Second, CON turned PRO's own design fix into a dilemma ("apprenticeship scales either small or bad"), which bites hard because the motion is explicitly about expansion; PRO's closing response effectively conceded fewer-but-better slots. Third, CON policed the metric: the proposition asks which raises long-run earnings more, and CON argued convincingly that PRO's bounded-downside case is largely a variance argument ("counts cash at 19, ignores exits at 30"), while expected value plus wage-slope and portability speak to the actual long-run level. PRO's best counter — that CON's case is a chain of conditionals — was neatly mirrored ("your single link is three links in disguise"). PRO's honesty and rhetoric were excellent, but CON left fewer live gaps and its closing sharpened the comparison rather than recapping it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's reply to the marginal-student test: subsidies do not merely push fence-sitters into debt but rescue already-enrolled students into completion, so PRO's "coin-flip completion" framing understates the payoff. PRO answered only by demanding an unavailable number, leaving the mechanism intact — reinforced by CON's scale dilemma that PRO's quality safeguards prevent the very expansion the motion requires.</best_rebuttal>
